l: Kibi, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: Kibi was the land of Princess Kuro’s native country. Emperor Nin-Toku made a progress there after following Princess Kuro.

l: Yamashiro, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: Yamashiro is a place with a river, Tsutsuki, and a boar-herd. The Empress withdrew there by ascending its river; Emperor Nin-Toku sent Toriyama and Kuchiko after her and later progressed there. Later, fleeing Kings Ohoke and Woke reached Karibawi, lost provisions, and crossed the River Kusuba toward Harima.

l: Yamato, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: Yamato is a land and high metropolis, mentioned in songs and journeys. Princess Kuro’s spouse went there, the Empress named it while passing Nara, and a song links it to a wild-goose’s egg. Emperor Ri-Chiu escaped there from a burning palace, and Midzu-ha-wake followed after killings. Emperor Yū-Riyaku called it the Island of the Dragon-Fly.

l: Nurinomi, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: Nurinomi, a person from Kara living at Tsutsuki, housed the Empress and explained her stay through strange insects he reared, which changed into creeping insects, cocoons, and flying birds.

l: Tsutsuki, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: Tsutsuki was where Nurinomi’s house stood and where the Empress stayed for some time. Kuchiko’s Song referred to the palace of Tsutsuki in Yamashiro.

l: Grandee of Wani, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: He was the Grandee of Wani whom Emperor Nin-Toku sent after the Empress. He reached Nurinomi’s house, endured heavy rain while trying to deliver the Emperor’s Song, and, with Princess Kuchi and Nurinomi, reported the reason for the Empress’s stay.

l: King Hayabusa-wake, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: Younger brother of Emperor Nin-Toku, Hayabusa-wake sought and married Queen Medori, fled with her when the Emperor raised an army, and was overtaken and slain at Soni in Uda.

l: Mount Kurahashi, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: Queen Medori and King Hayabusa-wake fled to Mount Kurahashi, whose steep, ladder-like rocks they described in Songs. The Imperial army pursued them from there and later slew them at Soni in Uda.

l: Emperor Ri-Chiu, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: Emperor Ri-Chiu is a Heavenly Sovereign who originally dwelt at the palace of Naniha, was secretly carried into Yamato after King Sumi-no-ye-no-naka-tsu burned that palace, and later ruled the Empire from Wakasakura at Ihare. He met Midzu-ha-wake at the temple of the Deity of Iso-no-kami, wed Princess Kuro, and had King Oshiha of Ichinobe, King Mima, and Awomi-no-iratsume. During his reign he made appointments, granted names, and established the Ihare Clan. He died at sixty-four and was buried at Mozu.

l: Ihare, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: The august mausoleum of Emperor Yōmei had been by the borders of Lake Ihare.

l: King Oshiha of Ichinobe, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: is_father_of Emperor Ken-Zō King Ichinobe was Emperor Ken-Zō's father. His august bones were sought out and recovered from the land of Afumi, identified in part by his uneven teeth, and interred before being brought up to the Capital.

l: palace of Naniha, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: Emperor Ri-Chiu dwelt at the palace of Naniha before King Sumi-no-ye-no-naka-tsu set fire to it while the Emperor was asleep after a feast.

l: King Sumi-no-ye-no-naka-tsu, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: Younger brother of Emperor Ri-Chiu, he burns the great palace while Ri-Chiu sleeps, then is deceived and killed by His Augustness Midzu-ha-wake.

l: Suzerain of Achi, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: Suzerain of Achi secretly rescues Emperor Ri-Chiu from a burning palace, leads him into Yamato, receives appointment as Treasurer and domains, and becomes ancestor of Suzerains of Aya in Yamato.

l: Ohosaka mountain, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: At the entrance of the Ohosaka mountain, Emperor Ri-Chiu's party met a woman who warned them that armed men blocked the direct route. His Augustness Midzu-ha-wake later halted there and killed Sobakari.

l: temple of the Deity of Isonokami, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: Emperor Ri-Chiu dwelt in the temple of the Deity of Isonokami after reaching Yamato. His Augustness Midzu-ha-wake later proceeded to the temple of the Deity of Iso-no-kami and reported that he had completed his assigned work.

l: His Augustness Midzu-ha-wake, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: His Augustness Midzu-ha-wake, younger brother of Emperor Ri-Chiu and also called Emperor Han-Zei, is a Heavenly sovereign who rules the Empire from the palace of Shibakaki at Tajihi. After rejecting King Sumi-no-ye-no-naka-tsu's intentions, he is ordered to kill him, appoints Sobakari Prime Minister, kills Sobakari, reaches Chika-tsu-Asuka, performs purification and worship, and serves Emperor Ri-Chiu. He marries Lady of Tsunu and Oto-hime and has four children, including Lady of Kahi, Lady of Tsubura, King Takara, and Lady of Takabe. He dies at sixty and has a mausoleum on the Moor of Mozu.

l: Sobakari, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: Sobakari, a man-at-arms serving King Sumi-no-ye-no-naka-tsu, kills his lord with a spear at His Augustness Midzu-ha-wake’s command. Appointed Prime Minister and honored, he is ultimately killed by His Augustness Midzu-ha-wake with a concealed sword.

l: copious feast at Hatsuse, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: is_a copious feast [held under a hundred-branching tsuki-tree at Hatsuse] At the copious feast at Hatsuse, held under a hundred-branching tsuki-tree, the female attendant from Mihe presented the great august cup to Emperor Yū-Riyaku. The attendant, the Empress, and the Emperor sang songs, and the attendant was praised and plentifully endowed.

l: burning of the great palace, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: The great palace at Naniha was set on fire by King Sumi-no-ye-no-naka-tsu while Emperor Ri-Chiu was asleep. The fire was still visible from the Pass of Hanifu as the Emperor was carried toward Yamato.

l: progress into Yamato, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: Progress into Yamato follows Emperor Ri-Chiu’s secret rescue from a burning palace and Midzu-ha-wake’s killing of King Sumi-no-ye-no-naka-tsu.

l: slaying of King Sumi-no-ye-no-naka-tsu, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: is_a slaying His Augustness Midzu-ha-wake carried out Emperor Ri-Chiu's command to slay King Sumi-no-ye-no-naka-tsu. Sobakari killed the King in the privy by thrusting him with a spear.

l: appointment of Sobakari as Prime Minister, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: is_a appointment His Augustness Midzu-ha-wake appointed Sobakari Prime Minister at a temporary palace near the entrance to the Ohosaka mountain. Sobakari was honored by the officials and believed that he had achieved his design.

l: killing of Sobakari, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: At Ohosaka mountain’s entrance, His Augustness Midzu-ha-wake appointed Sobakari Prime Minister, then drew a sword from beneath matting and beheaded him as he drank.

l: august mausoleum at Mozu, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: Emperor Ri-Chiu's august mausoleum is at Mozu.

l: Lady of Tsunu, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: Kogoto’s daughter marries Emperor Han-Zei and bears the Lady of Kahi and the Lady of Tsubura.

l: Kogoto, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: is_a Grandee [of Wani] Kogoto is Grandee of Wani and the father of the Lady of Tsunu and Oto-hime.

l: Oto-hime, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: is_a daughter [of Kogoto] Oto-hime is the daughter of Kogoto, Grandee of Wani. She marries Emperor Han-Zei and bears King Takara and the Lady of Takabe.

l: Emperor in-Giyō, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: Emperor in-Giyō ruled the Empire from the Palace of Toho-tsu-Asuka after recovering from a long sickness through a physician from Shiragi. He established surnames and gentile names, wed Empress Osaka-no-oho-naka-tsu-hime, had several august children, lived seventy-eight years, and was buried at Naga-ye near Wega in Kafuchi.

l: Empress Osaka-no-oho-naka-tsu-hime, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: is_younger_sister_of King Oho-hodo Empress Osaka-no-oho-naka-tsu-hime was the younger sister of King Oho-hodo and the wife of Emperor in-Giyō. She was among those who urged him to rule the Empire.

l: King Karu of Kinashi, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: King Karu of Kinashi was designated to rule after Emperor in-Giyō. After debauching his younger sister, Queen So-tohoshi, he lost official and public support, fled to the Noble Oho-mahe Wo-mahe’s house, was captured and banished to Iyo, then died with Queen So-tohoshi by killing themselves together.

l: His Augustness Anaho, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: His Augustness Anaho, a child of Emperor in-Giyō, ruled the Empire from the palace of Anaho at Isonokami. He raised and then disbanded an army against King Karu after a promise to deliver him. Later, persuaded by Grandee of Ne’s slander, he slew King Oho-kusaka and was beheaded in sleep by King Ma-yowa.

l: Karu-no-oho-iratsume, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: also_named Queen So-tohoshi Karu-no-oho-iratsume was a daughter of Emperor in-Giyō and the younger sister of King Karu of Kinashi. She was also called Sotohoshi-no-iratsume because the refulgence of her person passed through her garments.

l: Queen So-tohoshi, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: Queen So-tohoshi, also Karu-no-oho-iratsume and beloved spouse of King Karu of Kinashi, pursued him after banishment; unable to restrain love, they killed themselves together.

l: King Shiro-biko of Yatsuri, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: is_a King He was similarly unconcerned when told that Emperor an-Kō had been slain. Prince Oho-hatsuse dragged him away, buried him standing at Woharida, and he died when his eyes burst out as he was buried up to the loins.

l: His Augustness Oho-hatsuse, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: His Augustness Oho-hatsuse, younger brother of Emperor an-Kō and intended husband of Queen Waka-kusaka, ruled after an-Kō, slew several kings, and died with Grandee Tsubura during a siege.

l: surnames and gentile names, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: Emperor in-Giyō lamented transgressions in the surnames and gentile names of the people. He established the surnames and gentile names of the eighty heads of companies, including the Karu, Osaka, and Kaha Tribes.

l: the Empire, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: The Empire turns against King Karu of Kinashi after his incestuous relationship with his younger sister and turns towards His Augustness Anaho. It is then ruled in succession by Emperor Kim-Mei, Nu-na-kura-tama-shiki, His Augustness Tachibana-no-toyo-hi, Toyo-mike-kashiki-ya-hime, His Augustness Hatsuse-be-no-waka-sazaki, Nuna-kura-futo-tama-shiki, Emperor Yōmei, Emperor Su-Jun, and Empress Sui-Ko.

l: Grandee the Noble Oho-mahe Wo-mahe, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: secures King Karu of Kinashi [and presents him to His Augustness Anaho] The Grandee the Noble Oho-mahe Wo-mahe sheltered King Karu and made a provision of implements of war. He persuaded His Augustness Anaho not to attack King Karu, then secured King Karu and presented him to Anaho.

l: house of the Noble Oho-mahe Wo-mahe, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: contains implements of war [prepared for King Karu of Kinashi] The house of the Noble Oho-mahe Wo-mahe became King Karu's refuge, where he prepared implements of war. His Augustness Anaho later beleaguered the house before the Noble Oho-mahe intervened.

l: hot waters of Iyo, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: is_in Iyo The hot waters of Iyo were the place to which King Karu was banished.

l: Hatsuse, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: Hatsuse was the place of Emperor Yū-Riyaku’s palace and a location of his copious feast under a hundred-branching tsuki-tree. The Great Deity of Kadzuraki, Lord of One Word, escorted the Emperor to the entrance of the Hatsuse mountain.

l: songs, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: Songs in the Emperor in-Giyō records, sung by King Karu, Noble Oho-mahe Wo-mahe, Queen So-tohoshi, and His Augustness Anaho, unfold through Hind-Lifting, Rustic Lifting, Courtier's, Heaven-Soaring, Partly Lowered Rustic, and Reading styles.

l: death of Prince Karu and Princess So-Tohoshi, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: is_a death [the two killed themselves together] King Karu and Queen So-tohoshi killed themselves together after his banishment and her pursuit of him. Their final songs are identified as Reading Songs.

l: Grandee of Ne, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: Grandee sent by Emperor an-Kō to request Queen Waka-kusaka stole a ceremonial jewel headdress and falsely accused King Oho-kusaka of rejecting Imperial Commands.

l: Queen Waka-kusaka-be, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: is_a Queen Queen Waka-kusaka-be was the younger sister of King Oho-kusaka and had no children with Emperor Yū-Riyaku. When the Emperor sent her the white dog as a message, she said it was alarming that he had made a progress with his back to the sun and offered to come straight to the capital to serve him.

l: Empress, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: is_the_former_parent_of King Ma-yowa She was Nagata-no-oho-iratsume, the chief wife of King Oho-kusaka, whom Emperor an-Kō took and made Empress. Her former child was King Ma-yowa.

l: King Ma-yowa, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: King Ma-yowa, the Empress’s former child, overhears Emperor an-Kō fear his vengeance, then at seven waits for the sleeping emperor, beheads him with a sword, and flees to Grandee Tsubura’s house.

l: Grandee Tsubura, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: Grandee Tsubura, a householder with Princess Kara in service and five granaries, shelters fleeing King Ma-yowa; during Prince Oho-hatsuse’s siege, he fights until exhausted, kills Ma-yowa at his request, and cuts off his own head.

l: King Kurobiko, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: is_a King When Prince Oho-hatsuse asked what should be done after Emperor an-Kō was slain, King Kurobiko remained unconcerned. Prince Oho-hatsuse dragged him out and slew him.

l: Afumi, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: Afumi is a place containing Kuta, Wata, and the moor of Kaya at Wata, noted for abundant boars and deer where kings built temporary hunting palaces.

l: King Ichi-no-be-no-oshiha, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: King Ichi-no-be-no-oshiha, father of King Ohoke and King Woke, accompanied Prince Oho-hatsuse to Afumi, who killed, dismembered, and buried him beneath a horse’s manger.

l: King Ohoke, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: is_a King He was one of King Ichi-no-be-no-oshiha’s children. After his father was slain, he fled with King Woke, crossed into Harima, hid his person, and worked as a groom and cow-herd.

l: Prince Woke, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: Prince Woke, a younger brother of Prince Ohoke and child of King Ichi-no-be-no-oshiha, fled after his father’s death, hid in Harima, and worked as a groom and cow-herd. Later discovered with Ohoke, he was to wed Ofuwo, joined the Song-Hedge, helped besiege and slay Grandee Shibi, and became King by ruling the Empire after Ohoke ceded his claim.

l: land of Harima, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: contains Shizhimu [native of that country] Kings Ohoke and Woke entered Harima and hid in the house of a native named Shizhimu. They worked there as grooms and cow-herds.

l: slaying of King Oho-kusaka, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: The slaying of King Oho-kusaka occurs when Emperor an-Kō kills him after Grandee of Ne falsely claims he rejected Imperial Commands angrily.

l: slaying of Emperor an-Kō, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: King Ma-yowa, fearing Emperor an-Kō would avenge his father, overhears his fear and kills the sleeping Emperor with his sword.

l: slaying of King Kurobiko, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: Prince Oho-hatsuse slew King Kurobiko after finding him unconcerned about Emperor an-Kō’s slaying.

l: burial of King Shiro-biko, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: The burial of King Shiro-biko: Prince Oho-hatsuse dragged him to Woharida and buried him standing until, buried to the loins, he died and his eyes burst out.

l: siege of the house of Grandee Tsubura, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: Prince Oho-hatsuse besieges Grandee Tsubura’s house; fierce fighting exhausts Tsubura’s hands and arrows, then he kills Prince Ma-yowa at his request and himself.

l: death of King Ma-yowa, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: Death of King Ma-yowa: after slaying Emperor an-Kō and fleeing to Grandee Tsubura’s house, he is killed by Tsubura during Prince Oho-hatsuse’s siege.

l: death of Grandee Tsubura, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: Death of Grandee Tsubura, who killed Prince Ma-yowa at his request, then killed himself by cutting off his own head.

l: slaying of King Ichi-no-be-no-oshiha, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: Prince Oho-hatsuse followed King Ichi-no-be-no-oshiha to a hunting-ground, shot and dismembered him, placed him in a horse’s manger, and buried him.

l: flight of Kings Ohoke and Woke, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: After King Ichi-no-be-no-oshiha was slain, Kings Ohoke and Woke fled through Yamashiro, crossed the River Kusuba, and entered Harima.

l: hiding and servitude of Kings Ohoke and Woke, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: Kings Ohoke and Woke hide in Shizhimu’s Harima house, serving as grooms and cow-herds.

l: Emperor Yū-Riyaku, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: Emperor Yū-Riyaku, also called His Augustness Oho-hatsuse-no-waka-take and the Heavenly Sovereign Oho-hatsuse, dwelt at the palace of Asakura at Hatsuse and ruled the Empire. He married Queen Wake-kusaka-be, Queen Waka-kusaka-be, and Princess Karu; he fathered Shiraka and Princess Waka-tarashi. His life includes commands concerning Akawi-ko, a wedding at Yeshinu, progresses to Yeshinu and Mount Kadzuraki, reverence for the Great Deity of Kadzuraki, and a flagon from Princess Wodo. He established clans and retainers, hunted and composed songs, lived 124 years, and had slain King Ichinobe, provoking Ken-Zō’s wish for revenge.

l: Akawi-ko, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: Akawi-ko was a beautiful woman of the Hiketa Tribe whom Emperor Yū-Riyaku met washing clothes by the River Miwa. She awaited his command for eighty years, then brought tribute and sang four songs; he pitied her, declined marriage, and sent her home richly endowed.

l: Princess Wodo, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: Princess Wodo, daughter of Grandee Satsuki of Wani, is a Princess of Kasuga; Emperor Yū-Riyaku journeys to wed her, and she serves great liquor and sings a Quiet Song.

l: female attendant from Mihe, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: A female attendant from Mihe in Ise served Emperor Yū-Riyaku at a feast. When a leaf fell into his cup and he threatened her, she sang an explanation, won pardon, praise, and plentiful endowment.

l: Great Deity of Kadzuraki, Lord of One Word, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: The Great Deity of Kadzuraki, Lord of One Word, appeared on Mount Kadzuraki in a retinue indistinguishable from Emperor Yū-Riyaku’s. He identified himself as the Deity who dispels evil and good with a word, received the Emperor’s offerings, and escorted him to the entrance of the Hatsuse mountain.

l: palace of Asakura at Hatsuse, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: The palace of Asakura at Hatsuse was where Emperor Yū-Riyaku dwelt while ruling the Empire.

l: Kusaka, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: Kusaka was where the Empress dwelt in the beginning. Emperor Yū-Riyaku made a progress in Kafuchi by way of the Tadagoye road at Kusaka and later sang of Mount Kusakabe and Mount Heguri.

l: Yeshinu, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: Yeshinu was the destination of Emperor Yū-Riyaku’s progress. On the bank of the Yeshinu river he met and married a beautiful girl, and on a later visit he seated himself on an august throne, played the lute, and composed a song about her dancing.

l: Moor of Akidzu, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: was_named Akidzu-nu [after the dragon-fly incident] The Moor of Akidzu was where Emperor Yū-Riyaku hunted and sat on an august throne. After a horse-fly bit his arm and a dragon-fly ate the horse-fly, he composed a song, and the moor was thereafter called Akidzu-nu.

l: Mount Kadzuraki, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: Mount Kadzuraki was visited by Emperor Yū-Riyaku during a hunt and during an encounter with the Great Deity of Kadzuraki, Lord of One Word. On one visit he fled up an alder because of a wounded wild boar; on another, he encountered the deity’s matching retinue and offered his garments, sword, bow, and arrows.

l: Kasuga, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: Kasuga was where Emperor Yū-Riyaku made a progress to wed Princess Wodo, daughter of the Grandee Satsuki of Wani. A maiden hid beside a mound when she saw the Imperial progress, and the Emperor’s song gave the mound the name Mound of the Metal Spade.

l: Takawashi in Tajihi in Kafuchi, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: Takawashi in Tajihi in Kafuchi was the stated location of Emperor Yū-Riyaku’s august mausoleum.

l: Emperor Yū-Riyaku's mausoleum, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: Emperor Yū-Riyaku’s august mausoleum was at Takawashi in Tajihi in Kafuchi. Emperor Ken-Zō ordered it destroyed, but His Augustness Ohoke instead slightly excavated its side as an enduring token of insult.

l: horse-fly, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: is_a fly A horse-fly bit the august arm of Emperor Yū-Riyaku while he hunted at the Moor of Akidzu. A dragon-fly quickly ate it, and the Emperor composed a song about the event.

l: dragon-fly, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: ate horse-fly A dragon-fly came when a horse-fly bit Emperor Yū-Riyaku’s arm and ate the horse-fly. The Emperor’s song connected this deed with the naming of Yamato as the Island of the Dragon-Fly.

l: great august liquor, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: was_presented_at copious feast at Hatsuse The great august liquor was presented to Emperor Yū-Riyaku by the female attendant from Mihe and later by Princess Wodo. Songs were composed around its presentation at the feast.

l: Imperial progress to Mount Kadzuraki, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: During the Imperial progress to Mount Kadzuraki, Emperor Yū-Riyaku encountered a large wild boar and later a retinue resembling his own. The first incident led to a song about his flight up an alder, while the second led to the revelation and worshipful honoring of the Great Deity of Kadzuraki, Lord of One Word.

l: revelation of the Great Deity of Kadzuraki, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: The revelation of the Great Deity of Kadzuraki occurred when Emperor Yū-Riyaku encountered a matching retinue on the opposite acclivity of Mount Kadzuraki. The deity identified himself as the Great Deity of Kadzuraki, Lord of One Word, accepted the Emperor’s offerings, and escorted him toward Hatsuse.

l: Emperor Yū-Riyaku's death and burial, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: includes Emperor Yū-Riyaku's mausoleum The text does not narrate Emperor Yū-Riyaku’s death, but states that his august years were one hundred and twenty-four. It gives the location of his august mausoleum as Takawashi in Tajihi in Kafuchi.

l: His Augustness Shiraka-no-oho-yamato-ne-ko, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: His Augustness Shiraka-no-oho-yamato-ne-ko dwelt at Mikakuri palace in Ihare and ruled the Empire; having neither Empress nor children, his decease left no King to rule.

l: King, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: rules Empire [intended successor after Shiraka-no-oho-yamato-ne-ko's decease] After the decease of His Augustness Shiraka-no-oho-yamato-ne-ko, there was no King to rule the Empire.

l: search for a successor to Shiraka-no-oho-yamato-ne-ko, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: After Shiraka-no-oho-yamato-ne-ko’s decease, an enquiry seeks a King to rule the Empire and the sun’s succession, finding Oshinumi-no-iratsume at Tsunusashi’s palace in Oshinumi, Kadzuraki.

l: Oshinumi-no-iratsume, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: Oshinumi-no-iratsume, also called Princess Ihi-toyo, is the younger sister of Prince Ichinobe-oshiha-wake and aunt of Prince Ohoke and Prince Woke. She is found residing at the palace of Tsunusashi at Takaki in Oshinumi in Kadzuraki.

l: Wodate, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: Wodate, Chief of the Mountain Clan and governor of Harima, hears a younger brother’s song at Shizhimu’s rejoicing, recognizes two children as princes, drives away the cave’s people, provides them a temporary palace, and sends news to the capital.

l: elder brother (Prince Ohoke), Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: is_a young child [employed to light the fire] The elder brother was one of the two children discovered by Wodate. He later ceded the Empire to the younger brother, saying that the younger brother's deed had enabled them to become lords of the Empire.

l: younger brother (Prince Woke), Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: is_a young child [employed to light the fire] The younger brother was one of the two children discovered by Wodate and revealed their names through a chant at Shizhimu's rejoicing. He later ruled the Empire first after Prince Ohoke ceded it to him.

l: His Augustness Ohoke, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: His Augustness Ohoke, elder brother of Prince Woke and Emperor Ken-Zō, was discovered with Woke by Wodate. He joined Woke in counsel against Grandee Shibi, then ceded the Empire to Woke. He later slightly excavated Emperor Yū-Riyaku’s mausoleum and, after Ken-Zō’s death, ruled the succession of Heaven’s sun as Emperor Nin-Ken.

l: discovery of Princes Ohoke and Woke, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: is_made_by Wodate Wodate discovered Princes Ohoke and Woke when they were two young children employed to light the fire at Shizhimu's rejoicing in Harima. He recognized them from the younger brother's chant and brought them to the palace.

l: Grandee Shibi, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: Grandee Shibi, ancestor of the Grandees of Heguri, joins the Songs, takes Ofuwo’s hand and exchanges songs with Prince Woke, then angers him; the two princes besiege Shibi’s house and slay him.

l: Song-Hedge, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: The Song-Hedge was the exchange of songs between Grandee Shibi and Prince Woke. Shibi sang about the hedge of the child of a grandee and later threatened that the Prince's hedge would be cut and burnt.

l: siege and killing of Grandee Shibi, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: targets Grandee Shibi After taking counsel, Princes Ohoke and Woke raised an army, beleaguered the house of Grandee Shibi, and slew him.

l: government of the Empire, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: The government of the Empire was to be assumed by Princes Ohoke and Woke; after Grandee Shibi and Prince Woke exchanged songs, Ohoke ceded the Empire to Woke, resolving the succession.

l: ceding of the Empire by Prince Ohoke, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: is_made_to Prince Woke [younger brother] Prince Ohoke ceded the Empire to his younger brother Prince Woke because Woke had revealed their names at Shizhimu's house, enabling them to become lords of the Empire. Prince Woke therefore ruled the Empire first.

l: Emperor Ken-Zō, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: Emperor Ken-Zō, a Heavenly Sovereign, dwelt at the palace of Chika-tsu-Asuka and ruled the Empire for eight years. He wed Queen of Naniha but had no children, recovered King Ichinobe’s bones, punished a boar-herd, ordered disfigurement of Emperor Yū-Riyaku’s mausoleum, then died at thirty-eight and was buried at Ihatsuki.

l: old woman Oki-me, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: Oki-me, an old woman from Afumi, knew where King Ichinobe’s august bones were buried. Emperor Ken-Zō named her, built her a house near the palace, summoned her daily by the great-hall bell, and treated her kindly. She later departed for her native land.

l: august bones of King Ichinobe, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: The august bones of King Ichinobe were found after digging where Oki-me identified, interred in a mausoleum on the mountain east of the Moor of Kaya, and later brought to the Capital.

l: Emperor Nin-Ken, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: Emperor Nin-Ken, His Augustness Ohoke, was a Heavenly Sovereign who succeeded Emperor Ken-Zō, dwelt at Hirataka palace in Isono-kami, and ruled the Empire. He married Kasuga-no-oho-iratsume and then Naka-no-waku-go-no-iratsume, having seven children altogether.

l: Kasuga-no-oho-iratsume, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: Kasuga-no-oho-iratsume, Emperor Yū-Riyaku’s august daughter and Emperor Nin-Ken’s wife, is identified as mother of six children, including Wo-hatsuse-no-waka-sazaki and Prince Ma-waka.

l: His Grandeur Wo-hatsuse-no-waka-sazaki, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: His Grandeur Wo-hatsuse-no-waka-sazaki, also called Emperor Mu-Retsu, was a son of Emperor Nin-Ken and Kasuga-no-oho-iratsume, one of their seven august children. He afterwards became a Heavenly Monarch, dwelt at the palace of Namiki at Hatsuse, ruled the Empire for eight years, had no august children, and had a mausoleum on Ihatsuki mound at Karawoka.

l: death of Emperor Mu-Retsu, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: has_no_inheriting_prince prince (heir to the Empire) After the death of Emperor Mu-Retsu, there was no prince to inherit the Empire. Ohodo was therefore sent for from Afumi, married to Tashiraka, and presented with the Empire.

l: Emperor Kei-Tai, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: Emperor Kei-Tai, also called His Augustness Ohodo, was the fifth descendant of Heavenly Monarch Homuda. After Emperor Mu-Retsu’s death, he was sent for from Afumi, married Tashiraka, and received the Empire. Dwelling at Palace of Tamaho at Ihare, he ruled for forty-three years and had nineteen children.

l: Great Empress Tashiraka, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: Great Empress Tashiraka, daughter of Heavenly Monarch Ohoke, marries Ohodo after Emperor Mu-Retsu’s death as he receives the Empire.

l: His Augustness Hiro-kuni-oshi-taka-kana-hi, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: Child of Emperor Kei-Tai and Meko-no-iratsume, Hiro-kuni-oshi-taka-kana-hi succeeds him among rulers of the Empire.

l: His Augustness Take-wo-hiro-kuni-oshi-tate, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: His Augustness Take-wo-hiro-kuni-oshi-tate, Emperor Sen-Kuwa, child of Emperor Kei-Tai, dwelt at Ihorinu in Hinokuma and ruled the Empire. He had two wives and five august children, three by Tachi-bana-no-naka-tsu-hime and two by Kafuchi-no-waku-go-hime.

l: His Augustness Ame-kuni-oshi-haruki-hiro-niha, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: Child of Emperor Kei-Tai and Great Empress Tashiraka, Ame-kuni-oshi-haruki-hiro-niha afterwards ruled the Empire.

l: Queen Sasage, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: Queen Sasage, daughter of Emperor Kei-Tai and Wo-kumi-no-iratsume, served as presider at the temple of the Deity of Ise.

l: Ihawi, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: Ihawi, Lord of Tsukushi, defies Emperor Kei-Tai’s decrees, becomes subject of rebellion, and faces imperial envoys sent to slay him.

l: Mononobe-no-arakawi, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: is_a Great Chieftain Mononobe-no-arakawi, the Great Chieftain, was sent with Ohotomo-no-kanamura to slay Ihawi.

l: Ohotomo-no-kanamura, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: is_a Chieftain Ohotomo-no-kanamura, the Chieftain, was sent with Mononobe-no-arakawi to slay Ihawi.

l: rebellion of Ihawi, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: is_a rebellion Ihawi's rebellion consisted of his disobedience to the Imperial Decrees and his exceedingly disrespectful conduct during the reign of Emperor Kei-Tai.

l: sending of Mononobe-no-arakawi and Ohotomo-no-kanamura to slay Ihawi, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: Emperor Kei-Tai sends Mononobe-no-arakawi and Ohotomo-no-kanamura to slay Ihawi, Lord of Tsukushi.

l: reign of Emperor Kei-Tai, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: lasts forty-three years [august years] The reign of Emperor Kei-Tai lasted forty-three years. During it, Ihawi was disobedient to the Imperial Decrees and was exceedingly disrespectful.

l: Hiro-kuni-oshi-take-kana-hi, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: Hiro-kuni-oshi-take-kana-hi, Emperor Kan-an and a Heavenly Monarch, dwelt in Palace of Kanahashi, ruled Empire, had no august children, and was buried at Takaya.

l: Palace of Kanahashi, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: is_located_in Magari The Palace of Kanahashi was at Magari. Hiro-kuni-oshi-take-kana-hi dwelt there while ruling the Empire.

l: village of Takaya, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: is_in Furuchi The village of Takaya was in Furuchi in Kafuchi. It was the location of Hiro-kuni-oshi-take-kana-hi's august grave.

l: Her Augustness Tachi-bana-no-naka-tsu-hime, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: Wife of Emperor Sen-Kuwa and daughter of Heavenly Sovereign Ohoke, she bore Ishi-hime, Wo-ishi-hime, and King Kura-no-waka-ye.

l: Her Augustness Ishi-hime, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: Her Augustness Ishi-hime was an august child born to Emperor Sen-Kuwa by Her Augustness Tachi-bana-no-naka-tsu-hime.

l: Her Augustness Wo-ishi-hime, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: Her Augustness Wo-ishi-hime was an august child born to Emperor Sen-Kuwa by Her Augustness Tachi-bana-no-naka-tsu-hime.

l: King Kura-no-waka-ye, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: King Kura-no-waka-ye was an august child born to Emperor Sen-Kuwa by Her Augustness Tachi-bana-no-naka-tsu-hime.

l: Kafuchi-no-waku-go-hime, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: is_a wife [of Emperor Sen-Kuwa; next wife] Kafuchi-no-waku-go-hime was the next wife of Emperor Sen-Kuwa. She bore King Honoho and King Weha.

l: King Honoho, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: is_ancestor_of the Dukes Shihida King Honoho was an august child of Emperor Sen-Kuwa by Kafuchi-no-waku-go-hime. He was the ancestor of the Dukes Shihida.

l: King Weha, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: King Weha, child of Emperor Sen-Kuwa and Kafuchi-no-waku-go-hime, became ancestor of the Dukes of Wina and Tajihi.

l: the august children of Emperor Sen-Kuwa, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: Emperor Sen-Kuwa’s five august children, born to Tachi-bana-no-naka-tsu-hime and Kafuchi-no-waku-go-hime, included three Kings and two Queens.

l: Emperor Kim-Mei, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: Emperor Kim-Mei, a Heavenly Sovereign, dwelt in Shikishima, ruled the Empire, and had twenty-five children by five wives.

l: Nu-na-kura-tama-shiki, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: Child of Emperor Kim-Mei and Ishi-hime, Nu-na-kura-tama-shiki afterward ruled the Empire as King.

l: His Augustness Tachibana-no-toyo-hi, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: His Augustness Tachibana-no-toyo-hi, Emperor Yōmei, was a child of Emperor Kim-Mei who succeeded Nu-na-kura-tama-shiki. A Heavenly Sovereign, he dwelt in the Palace of Ikenobe and ruled the Empire for three years. He had wives Oho-gitashi-hime, Princess Hashi-bito-no-anaho-be, and Ihime-no-ko, and seven named children. He has the august mausoleum of Emperor Yōmei.

l: Toyo-mike-kashiki-ya-hime, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: Toyo-mike-kashiki-ya-hime, an august child of Emperor Kim-Mei, became Empress Sui-Ko and ruled the Empire after His Augustness Tachibana-no-toyo-hi. Wife and half-sister of Nuna-kura-futo-tama-shiki, she bore eight children, dwelt at the Palace of Wohorida, and ruled for thirty seven years.

l: His Augustness Hatsuse-be-no-waka-sazaki, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: King and child of Emperor Kim-Mei, His Augustness Hatsuse-be-no-waka-sazaki ruled the Empire after Toyo-mike-kashiki-ya-hime.

l: rule of the Empire, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: has_rulers four Kings and Queens The rule of the Empire passed successively from Emperor Kim-Mei to Nu-na-kura-tama-shiki, then to His Augustness Tachibana-no-toyo-hi, Toyo-mike-kashiki-ya-hime, and His Augustness Hatsuse-be-no-waka-sazaki. In all, four Kings and Queens ruled the Empire.

l: Nuna-kura-futo-tama-shiki, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: Nuna-kura-futo-tama-shiki is a Heavenly Sovereign who dwelt in the Palace of Wosada and ruled the Empire for fourteen years. He had four wives, including half-sister Toyo-mike-kashiki-ya-hime, and many children, including Hiko-hito among seventeen Kings and Queens. His august mausoleum is at Shinaga in Kafuchi.

l: Palace of Wosada, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: The Palace of Wosada was where Nuna-kura-futo-tama-shiki dwelt while ruling the Empire.

l: King Tame, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: King Tame was the one august child born to Emperor Yōmei by Oho-gitashi-hime, daughter of the Prime Minister.

l: Hiko-hito, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: Hiko-hito, husband and half-brother of Tamura, fathers three children with her, including a Heavenly Sovereign.

l: Tamura, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: Tamura, also called Nukade-hime, was Hiko-hito’s wife and half-sister and bore him three august children.

l: the Heavenly Sovereign that ruled the Empire from the Palace of Wokamoto, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: A Heavenly Sovereign, one of Hiko-hito and Queen Tamura’s three august children, ruled the Empire from the Palace of Wokamoto.

l: Palace of Wokamoto, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: The Palace of Wokamoto was where the Heavenly Sovereign mentioned in this unit ruled the Empire.

l: Shinaga, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: is_in Kafuchi Shinaga in Kafuchi was the location of the august mausoleum of Nuna-kura-futo-tama-shiki.

l: the august mausoleum of Nuna-kura-futo-tama-shiki, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: is_located_at Shinaga [in Kafuchi] The august mausoleum of Nuna-kura-futo-tama-shiki is at Shinaga in Kafuchi.

l: Palace of Ikenobe, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: The Palace of Ikenobe was where Emperor Yōmei dwelt while ruling the Empire.

l: Princess Hashi-bito-no-anaho-be, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: Princess Hashi-bito-no-anaho-be was Emperor Yōmei's next wife and his half-sister. She bore him Uhe-no-miya-no-uma-ya-dono-toyo-to-mimi, King Kume, King We-kuri, and King Mamuta.

l: Uhe-no-miya-no-uma-ya-dono-toyo-to-mimi, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: Uhe-no-miya-no-uma-ya-dono-toyo-to-mimi was one of the four august children born to Emperor Yōmei by Princess Hashi-bito-no-anaho-be.

l: Ihime-no-ko, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: Ihime-no-ko was Emperor Yōmei's next wife and the daughter of Tagima-no-kura-bito-hiro. She bore him King Tagima and Sugashiroko-no-iratsume.

l: august mausoleum of Emperor Yōmei, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: Emperor Yōmei’s august mausoleum stood by Lake Ihare’s borders before being removed to Shinaga’s middle sepulchre.

l: middle sepulchre of Shinaga, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: The middle sepulchre of Shinaga became the later location of Emperor Yōmei's august mausoleum.

l: Emperor Yōmei's reign, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: lasts three years Emperor Yōmei's reign lasted three years, during which he dwelt in the Palace of Ikenobe and ruled the Empire.

l: removal of Emperor Yōmei's mausoleum, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: Emperor Yōmei's mausoleum was removed from the borders of Lake Ihare to the middle sepulchre of Shinaga.

l: Emperor Su-Jun, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: Emperor Su-Jun, also called the Heavenly Sovereign Hatsuse-be-no-waka-sazaki, dwelt at the Palace of Shibabaki, ruled four years, and has a mausoleum on Kurahashi mound.

l: Kurahashi, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: Kurahashi was the location of the Palace of Shibabaki, where Emperor Su-Jun dwelt. The mound of Kurahashi contains his august mausoleum.

l: Palace of Wohorida, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: The Palace of Wohorida was where Empress Sui-Ko dwelt.

l: mausoleum, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume III (Emperor Nin-toku to Empress Sui-ko)
s: Empress Sui-Ko’s mausoleum stood on the mound of Ohonu before removal to the great sepulchre at Shinaga.

l: Kojiki, Kojiki
s: Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume II (Emperor Jim-mu to Emperor Ō-jin), translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain Vol. II. Sect.
